title: The LaBarbera family band and stock arrangements
summary: The brothers began in the family band at six or seven, playing stock dance-band arrangements; the stocks are explained as convertible, expandable arrangements.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Excellent. I’m not going to spend a lot of time on this but I had a couple of thoughts and questions about the family band. For those of you who might be watching we have three brothers and your father and mother were also in the group. Is that correct?
And how old were you during the years that this band was active?

I think I started when I was six or seven. If Pat was eight then I was six. And Joe would have been, oh no, I think I was seven and Joe was five, or four. I’m sorry. Joe was four or five. Somewhere along in that line. It’s hard to remember because we were always playing. The family band came much — but my mother at first was not part of the band as you probably know from Pat. But I think when I was about eight we were gigging steadily as a family band.
Did your father write parts for your trumpet playing that — with the fact that you’re seven or eight?

No, no. We just played stock arrangements. We didn’t ease into it. I mean they weren’t that difficult, the stocks weren’t that difficult but we started right out playing stocks. He wrote some polka things out that — he would transcribe some polka parts for the trumpet that were originally for me, and he made the clarinet or mandolin — Pat would play clarinet and I would play, well during those — when we played the polkas I played piano most of the time. But he would copy some parts, yeah, for trumpet, but not a lot.
For the folks who don’t know, can you explain what stocks means?
Oh, well, these were dance band arrangements. They were called convertible arrangements. I called them contemptible, contemptible, but anyway these arrangements © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

were written for a typical society dance band which included violin; piano, bass and drums; saxophones, so you would have your first alto, your second tenor, and the third part would be baritone sometimes. All right? And two trumpets and one trombone. Usually. And they were expandable, also expendable. So you could play them with a trumpet and an alto saxophone, first trumpet and first alto, and rhythm section, and they would sound. But then you could add all those other instruments and they’d sound fuller. And this is the type of arranging that we used to use for the Catskill Mountain singers you know, they want to play it with a trio and a full big band. It’s got to be expandable. And it’s a certain technique that was — Spud Murphy, Johnny Warrington, all those guys could write these things, Van Alexander. And they were quite popular. And my father, we would go every week to Rochester, New York to Levitt’s Music and he would buy more stocks, whatever the popular tune was, and we’d play it. I’ve got them all in my garage.
